Front: How would you explain Java as an ecosystem rather than only a language?
Back: Java includes the language, compiler, JVM, standard library, build tools, frameworks, and community ecosystem.
Extra: This matters because real Java development usually involves tools like Maven/Gradle and frameworks like Spring, not only `.java` syntax.

Front: Why does Java's object-oriented model matter early in learning?
Back: Most Java code is written inside classes, and programs are structured around objects that combine data and behavior.
Extra: Later topics such as encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, and interfaces depend on this mental model. Review it by naming the rule, one concrete Java consequence, and one mistake this card helps prevent. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/getStarted/intro/definition.html.

Front: What is wrong with saying "Java code runs everywhere"?
Back: It skips the JVM layer: Java source is compiled into bytecode, and bytecode runs on compatible JVMs.
Extra: Better wording: Java bytecode can run on many platforms that provide a compatible JVM. Review it by naming the rule, one concrete Java consequence, and one mistake this card helps prevent. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/getStarted/intro/definition.html.

Front: Why is the JVM not platform independent even though Java is called platform independent?
Back: A JVM implementation is built for a specific OS and CPU architecture.
Extra: The bytecode is portable; each platform needs its own JVM implementation to execute it. Review it by naming the rule, one concrete Java consequence, and one mistake this card helps prevent. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/getStarted/intro/definition.html.

Front: How does Java reduce some dangerous memory errors compared with C/C++?
Back: Java avoids normal pointer arithmetic and uses automatic memory management.
Extra: This does not remove all bugs, but it reduces direct invalid memory access patterns common in lower-level languages.

Front: Why does Garbage Collection not mean memory is irrelevant?
Back: Garbage Collection only reclaims unreachable objects; code can still keep unnecessary references alive.
Extra: Example: a static list that keeps accumulating objects can prevent those objects from being collected. Review it by naming the rule, one concrete Java consequence, and one mistake this card helps prevent. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/getStarted/intro/definition.html.

Front: Why is Java suitable for long-running server applications?
Back: Java has a stable runtime, strong ecosystem, automatic memory management, multithreading support, and runtime optimization through the JVM.
Extra: Stable runtime means the JVM is mature, predictable, well-tested, and supported for production use. This matters because backend services may run for weeks or months, so memory management, JIT behavior, monitoring, compatibility, and crash resistance need to be reliable. JIT warm-up can also improve performance after frequently used code paths are optimized.

Front: Why can multithreading be both useful and dangerous?
Back: It enables concurrent work but can introduce race conditions, deadlocks, and difficult debugging problems.
Extra: This is why Java has a dedicated concurrency topic later in the roadmap. Review it by naming the rule, one concrete Java consequence, and one mistake this card helps prevent. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/getStarted/intro/definition.html.

Front: How would you answer "Is Java related to JavaScript?" in an interview?
Back: They are different languages with different runtime models and ecosystems.
Extra: The similar names are mostly historical/marketing, not a sign that the languages are closely related. Review it by naming the rule, one concrete Java consequence, and one mistake this card helps prevent. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/getStarted/intro/definition.html.

Front: What is the practical difference between JDK and JRE?
Back: The JDK is for building Java programs; the JRE is for running Java programs.
Extra: If `javac` is missing, you likely do not have a full JDK available on PATH. Review it by naming the rule, one concrete Java consequence, and one mistake this card helps prevent. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/getStarted/intro/definition.html.

Front: How are JVM, JRE, and JDK related?
Back: The JDK includes development tools and runtime components; the JRE provides runtime libraries and the JVM; the JVM executes bytecode.
Extra: Memory rule: JVM runs bytecode, JRE runs apps, JDK builds apps. Review it by naming the rule, one concrete Java consequence, and one mistake this card helps prevent. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/getStarted/intro/definition.html.

Front: Why is installing only a runtime not enough for Java development?
Back: A runtime can run Java applications, but development also needs tools such as `javac` to compile source code.
Extra: This is why learners should install a JDK, not just a runtime. Review it by naming the rule, one concrete Java consequence, and one mistake this card helps prevent. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/getStarted/intro/definition.html.

Front: What is the difference between `java` and `javac`?
Back: `javac` compiles source code into bytecode; `java` runs compiled classes on the JVM.
Extra: Do not say `javac` runs Java programs or that `java` compiles source files. Review it by naming the rule, one concrete Java consequence, and one mistake this card helps prevent. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/getStarted/intro/definition.html.

Front: What happens when you run `javac HelloWorld.java`?
Back: The compiler checks the source code and produces `HelloWorld.class` if compilation succeeds.
Extra: Compilation errors stop this process before runtime begins. Review it by naming the rule, one concrete Java consequence, and one mistake this card helps prevent. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/getStarted/intro/definition.html.

Front: What happens when you run `java HelloWorld`?
Back: The JVM starts, loads the `HelloWorld` class, finds the main method, and executes the program.
Extra: You pass the class name `HelloWorld`, not the file name `HelloWorld.class`. Review it by naming the rule, one concrete Java consequence, and one mistake this card helps prevent. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/getStarted/intro/definition.html.

Front: Why is bytecode not the same as native machine code?
Back: Bytecode is an intermediate JVM instruction format, while native machine code is CPU-specific code.
Extra: The JVM can interpret bytecode or compile hot bytecode into native code using JIT. Review it by naming the rule, one concrete Java consequence, and one mistake this card helps prevent. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/getStarted/intro/definition.html.

Front: Why does bytecode verification matter?

Front: Why can Java speed improve after the application has been running for a while?

Front: How does `text = null` relate to Garbage Collection?
Back: It removes one reference to the object. If no other references remain, the object may become eligible for Garbage Collection.
Extra: It does not immediately collect the object; GC timing is controlled by the JVM. Review it by naming the rule, one concrete Java consequence, and one mistake this card helps prevent. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/getStarted/intro/definition.html.

Front: What is the key difference between compile-time and runtime errors?

Extra: `int age = "eighteen";` is compile-time. `10 / 0` is runtime. Review it by naming the rule, one concrete Java consequence, and one mistake this card helps prevent. Reference: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/getStarted/intro/definition.html.

Front: Why is `int age = "eighteen";` rejected before the program runs?

Front: Why can `int result = 10 / 0;` compile but still fail?
